source: An et al. (2025) Enhancing Student Learning with LLM-Generated Retrieval Practice Questions: Data Science Courses
finding: Students got LLM-written multiple-choice retrieval questions after each lecture segment, with feedback. Their quiz score was higher than in a control cycle with no in-lecture retrieval.
numbers: About 60 undergrads, analysed n=31 (Quiz 1, practice) vs n=27 (Quiz 2, control). Mean 0.89 vs 0.73 (SD 0.13 vs 0.15), median 0.95 vs 0.75. Mann-Whitney U=703, p<0.0001, rank-biserial r=0.586. Questions after each 10-15 min segment, immediate feedback, unlimited retries.
limits: Non-randomised, two cycles, Quiz 1 and Quiz 2 covered different material. Same students analysed as independent groups. Ceiling effect (median 0.95). Only about 2 weeks of delay. No restudy control, only 'nothing'.
agent_relevance: Humans only. Shows LLMs can supply the question side of the testing effect. Our agent has no forgetting, so the benefit does not transfer directly.

source: An et al. (2025) same paper: question-generation pipeline and quality
finding: Questions were made by Gemini 2.0/2.5 Flash from lecture notebooks. Free ChatGPT (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o) gave no significant difference in early comparison. Instructors checked every item.
numbers: Prompt asked for at least 15 MCQs per input, one correct answer plus three distractors, mixed recall and higher-order levels, with explanation. Roughly two-thirds of generated MCQs failed the authors' standards before review.
limits: Human review time not measured, so claimed time saving is unquantified.
agent_relevance: LLM question generation needs a verifier. If our agent self-quizzes, it needs a check on the quizzes it writes (a failing rate near two-thirds is a warning).

source: Leong, Rose, Dierker, Laverghetta (2026) A Feasibility Study on Retrieval Practice Using Large Language Models (AIME-Con)
finding: First direct comparison of LLM-written vs instructor-written retrieval practice items in a real course. LLM items were easier and less discriminating.
numbers: Intro psychology course, more than 700 students, within-subject mix, six quiz weeks. 30 LLM items (after review of 93; from gpt-oss-20b, GPT-5-mini, Qwen3-Next-80B; 9, 7 and 14 items) vs 30 instructor items. Mean difference LLM minus human: difficulty -1.01 (posterior probability lower about 1.0), discrimination -0.19 (probability 0.94).
quote: LLM-generated items exhibited overall weaker psychometric properties
limits: One topic, one instructor reviewer, small and cheap models, simple zero/few-shot prompts. Sparse data for LLM items.
agent_relevance: Easier items mean less effortful retrieval, which is the very thing the testing effect needs. A self-quizzing loop should ask for hard items and check difficulty.

source: Leong et al. (2026) same paper: structure, latency and criterion validity
finding: Despite being easier, LLM items looked similar to human items on length and speed, and predicted final exam score a bit less well.
numbers: Length: Mann-Whitney U=483, p=0.63. Flesch reading ease median 26.97 (LLM) vs 41.48 (human), U=576.5, p=0.06. Log response time effect d=0.05, chi2(1)=1.83, p=0.18. Correlation with final exam: human r=0.20 (p=0.003), LLM r=0.15 (p=0.03), Steiger z=0.76, p=0.45. Human vs LLM RP scores r=0.41.
limits: Final exam covered all topics, the items covered one, so correlations are capped low. Differences not significant.
agent_relevance: Surface features (length, speed) hide quality gaps. Do not judge self-made practice items by how they look.

source: Leong et al. (2026) same paper: prior work summary (Yusof 2025; An et al. 2025)
finding: The paper lists only two earlier studies of LLM retrieval practice, and says neither used a human-item RP control.
numbers: Yusof (2025): measurement and evaluation course, n=64, LLM RP group had significantly higher final exam than no-RP control. An et al. (2025): n about 120 across two courses, RP better than none.
limits: Second-hand description. Yusof 2025 itself not opened.
agent_relevance: Evidence that LLM-delivered retrieval practice helps humans is thin: two small quasi-experiments with no-practice controls.

source: Tullis, Heshmati, Burross, van Dorn (2026) Using Generative AI to Support Retrieval Practice (CogSci 48)
finding: Texts were reread or studied with AI-made questions plus AI feedback. At a delay, the AI retrieval group answered more questions right than rereaders. Tested by multiple choice or short answer, immediate or delayed.
numbers: Only the abstract and first page were readable in the downloaded file. No numbers were extracted.
limits: Abstract-level only. Sample size and effect size unknown to me.
agent_relevance: Best current match to the classic restudy-vs-retrieval design with an LLM as question writer and feedback giver. Pattern (gain at delay) matches the human literature.

source: An and Wang (2026) Student Use of LLMs and the Limits of AI-Generated Question Difficulty in Data Science Courses
finding: LLM-assigned Easy/Medium/Hard labels and Bloom levels did not predict how hard students found the items.
numbers: 378 authored MCQs, 311 deployed, 7,888 student responses, three courses. Label vs Bloom level rho=0.90. Label vs empirical difficulty rho=0.06, Bloom level rho=0.02. Students reported satisfaction and time savings but perceived deep-learning benefit fell over the term and over-reliance was noted.
limits: Read from abstract page only. LLM name not stated there.
agent_relevance: LLMs cannot self-rate item difficulty. The rule 'harder successful retrieval helps more' cannot be applied by asking the model how hard a question is.

source: Elkins, Kochmar, Cheung, Serban (2025) How Teachers Can Use LLMs and Bloom's Taxonomy to Create Educational Quizzes
finding: GPT-3.5 generated question candidates by Bloom level. 24 teachers wrote quizzes by hand, with simple-prompt candidates, or with Bloom-controlled candidates. Quality was no lower with generated help, and some metrics were better.
numbers: 24 teachers (12 per domain, biology and machine learning), 12 passages per domain, each teacher wrote 3 quizzes of 5-10 questions. Proportion unanswerable 0.08-0.12, disfluent 0.08-0.14, irrelevant 0-0.05 across types. Quiz-writing time about the same. Annotator Kendall tau mostly above 0.5, many above 0.81.
limits: Teacher and annotator ratings, no student learning measured. Earlier work cited there: final global acceptance of generated questions only 52%.
agent_relevance: Supports LLM as question author with human review. Says nothing about learner gains.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) Instruction-tuned Language Models are Better Knowledge Learners (pre-instruction-tuning, PIT)
finding: Closest LLM parallel to practice-test-then-study. Training on question-answer pairs before training on documents lifted closed-book QA more than the standard order. Perplexity on documents falls to near 1 but QA stays low.
numbers: Llama-2 7B / 70B, Wiki2023-film, exact match. Closed-book 9.5/17.2. Continued pretraining 27.6/41.7. Pretrain then instruction-tune 30.3/46.4. PIT 45.4/62.7. PIT++ (7B) 48.1, +17.8 points over standard. QA first vs after, 7B: grouped 38.2 vs 27.2, interleaved 45.9 vs 43.2.
limits: Wikipedia only, Llama-2 only, factual recall. The authors do not claim a link to the testing effect. The link is my analogy.
agent_relevance: Learning how knowledge will be asked for helps absorption. For a scaffold with a frozen model, the analogue is putting the questions before the material in the prompt, not training.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) PIT ablations: forgetting and token weighting
finding: Gains are not explained by less forgetting or by upweighting answer tokens.
numbers: Mixing test docs into instruction tuning: 30.2 EM (no gain). Weighted continued pretraining 27.7. Epochs 1/3/5/10: 33.3/45.4/45.8/46.5. Cross-domain 7B/70B: standard 23.6/42.8 vs PIT 36.9/55.2. Real Google 'People Also Ask' questions (93, 7B): 21.5 vs 29.0.
limits: Small real-question set. Some table and text values differ slightly (45.4 vs 45.5).
agent_relevance: The effect comes from question-shaped exposure, not from extra repetition. Compare the human finding that retrieval beats restudy at equal exposure.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Self-Tuning: Instructing LLMs to Effectively Acquire New Knowledge through Self-Teaching
finding: Extends PIT: documents are presented for memorisation plus self-made comprehension and self-reflection tasks (summaries, gap-fill, etc.). It beat PIT on new-knowledge extraction.
numbers: Llama2-7B, Wiki-Bio extraction exact match as read from the garbled table: continued pretraining 3.62, standard instruction tuning 5.13, PIT 11.61, Self-Tuning 31.52. Document perplexity about 1.11 for Self-Tuning vs 2.08 for PIT.
limits: Table text was extracted from the PDF with misaligned rows, so figures carry moderate confidence. Llama-2 7B and Wikipedia-2023 only.
agent_relevance: Self-generated questions and reflections on the material (a self-testing loop) work better than plain reading. Nearest machine analogue of generation plus retrieval, but done by training.

source: Memory GAPS: Would LLMs pass the Tulving Test? (2024)
finding: A 7B instruction model was given a 48-word list, then recognised and recalled it with copy, associate, rhyme and unrelated cues. It did not behave like people. After a delay it lost the studied list.
numbers: mistral-7b-instruct-v0, 384 observations per cell. Immediate recognition: copy 1.00, others 0.00. Delayed recognition false alarms 0.41-0.50 for non-copy cues. Immediate recall of copy cues 0.46 (humans 0.69). Delayed recall of copy cues 0.00, associates 0.40 (humans 0.37).
limits: One model. Human numbers from Tulving 1983 with a different procedure. Text and table disagree on one cell. Explanations untested.
agent_relevance: A model's 'memory' of an in-context list is not like a human trace, and cued recall can be dominated by pretrained semantics. Do not assume human recall effects on in-context lists.

source: Zhong et al. (2023) MemoryBank: Enhancing LLMs with Long-Term Memory (AAAI 2024)
finding: Agent memory with Ebbinghaus-style decay. A memory item's strength S rises by 1 and elapsed time resets to 0 each time it is recalled in a conversation. So each successful retrieval strengthens a trace.
numbers: R = exp(-t/S). Evaluation: 10 days of dialogue, 15 virtual users, human scoring of recall, with ChatGPT, ChatGLM and BELLE based SiliconFriend. Mostly qualitative examples.
limits: No ablation of the forgetting rule in what I read. Quantitative section is human scoring on a small set.
agent_relevance: Retrieval-strengthens-memory rule used inside an agent loop. Our agent keeps everything, so decay is only useful if memory gets too large or noisy.

source: Settles and Meeder (2016) A Trainable Spaced Repetition Model for Language Learning (half-life regression)
finding: Duolingo fitted a half-life model of word memory from log data. It predicted recall far better than the Leitner and Pimsleur schedules and raised student activity in a live test.
numbers: 12.9 million student-word traces, 90/10 split. MAE: HLR 0.128, Leitner 0.235, Pimsleur 0.445, constant baseline 0.175 (error cut by more than 45%). Abstract: improved an engagement measure by 12% in an operational user study.
limits: Predicts recall and engagement, not delayed test performance. Word learning in one app.
agent_relevance: Old AI system built on the spacing and testing literature. Retrieval outcomes drive scheduling. Only useful to us for any component that forgets or truncates.

source: Tabibian, Upadhyay, De, Zarezade, Scholkopf, Gomez-Rodriguez (2019) Enhancing human learning via spaced repetition optimization (PNAS; arXiv 1712.01856)
finding: Posed review scheduling as optimal control. The best review rate is proportional to the forgetting probability. Algorithm Memorize beat uniform and threshold schedules on Duolingo data and synthetic data.
numbers: Forgetting models: exponential and power-law. Each review is a test whose recall result updates the forgetting rate. Evaluated by likelihood of recorded Duolingo schedules, not a live randomised trial in what I read.
limits: Observational comparison on logs. The abstract says only 'may be able to help'.
agent_relevance: A formal link between testing and scheduling. Again requires a forgetting process.

source: Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne, Ponti (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning (Sci Rep 15:17458)
finding: Randomised crossover trial of a custom AI tutor against in-class active learning in Harvard physics. Tutor group learned more in less time. The tutor was built on pedagogy (active engagement, cognitive load, scaffolding) but is not a pure retrieval-practice test.
numbers: N=194 in a course of 233. Post-test median 4.5 (N=142 AI) vs 3.5 (N=174 in-class); pre-test median 2.75. Rank-sum z=-5.6, p<1e-8. Effect size 0.63 (regression) to about 0.73 (quantile). Median time on task 49 minutes.
limits: Not retrieval practice specifically. Short immediate post-test. One course.
agent_relevance: Tutor design matters more than model power. Not evidence for the testing effect itself.

source: Yuan, Su, Yao (2026) Diagnosing Retrieval vs Utilization Bottlenecks in LLM Agent Memory (ICLR 2026 workshop)
finding: Related only by name. In agent memory the choice of retrieval method mattered far more than the write strategy. Cheap raw storage matched costlier summary or fact extraction.
numbers: LoCoMo, 3 write strategies x 3 retrieval methods. Accuracy ranged 57.1% to 77.2% across retrieval methods (about 20 points). Write strategy differences 3 to 8 points.
limits: Abstract page only. This is memory retrieval for a system, not retrieval practice by a learner.
agent_relevance: Do not confuse system retrieval with learner retrieval. Still, retrieving well beats elaborate storing.

source: Pan et al. (2019) Pretesting versus posttesting (via search snippet)
finding: Human contrast for the PIT parallel: pre-testing helps less than post-testing and did not transfer to untested items.
numbers: Snippet: post-testing d=0.74, pre-testing d=0.35.
limits: Seen only in a search summary; not opened.
agent_relevance: Warns that question-first (PIT-like) gains in machines may not match human pretesting limits.

source: Rickard and Pan (2017) dual memory theory of the testing effect (via search snippet)
finding: Competing explanation: study events and test events form separate memories, so retrieval gains come from two traces.
numbers: No numbers taken.
limits: Only a search listing. Not opened.
agent_relevance: A two-trace view fits an agent that logs attempts and answers separately.

source: Retrieval vs restudy effect size summary (2024 artificial-language paper, via search snippet)
finding: A search summary quotes a range for the retrieval vs restudy effect.
numbers: Hedges g = 0.50 to 0.63 (as summarised). Source details unverified.
limits: Not opened. The listed URL may not be the exact paper.
agent_relevance: Background magnitude only.

source: Marketing course RAG tutor (AERA 2026 abstract, via search snippet)
finding: A retrieval-augmented GenAI tutor in an introductory marketing course found no significant differences in the outcomes measured.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Conference abstract in a snippet, not opened. A null result.
agent_relevance: Null results exist for LLM tutors. Weighs against assuming any AI helper gives a testing-type gain.

source: Naval Postgraduate School report on LLM test generation (via search snippet)
finding: Concluded that LLM test generation is currently unreliable and manual methods are still needed.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Consistent with the high reject rates for generated items in c02.

source: Large-scale field study of AI-generated exams (arXiv, via aitopics snippet)
finding: Reported AI-made exam questions can be of good quality.
numbers: About 1,700 students, 91 classes (as summarised).
limits: Snippet only. Measures exam quality, not a testing effect.
agent_relevance: Background for item quality at scale.

source: Allen-Zhu and Li (2023) Physics of Language Models 3.1: Knowledge Storage and Extraction (not opened)
finding: From prior knowledge: models extract facts reliably only if training text was augmented with varied rewrites or QA, even when memorised.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session. Unverified.
agent_relevance: Suggests knowledge must be practised in the format it will be asked for.

source: Pavlik and Anderson (2008) Using a model to compute the optimal schedule of practice (not opened)
finding: From prior knowledge: an ACT-R activation model gives optimal practice spacing for retrieval practice.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Unverified.
agent_relevance: Early cognitive-model basis for spaced retrieval schedulers.

source: Search finding: no controlled study of a testing effect in LLM learners themselves
finding: Five web searches and three arXiv listing searches (testing effect, retrieval practice, spacing, LLM) found no study testing whether in-context or fine-tuned LLMs show a human-like retrieval-vs-restudy effect.
numbers: Listings for 'testing effect' returned mostly software-testing papers.
limits: Absence evidence. Tools were limited (arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex rate limited). Could be missed.
agent_relevance: Gap. Our agent has no forgetting, so a testing effect is not expected; any gain would come from verification, not memory strengthening.

source: Synthesis of PIT and Self-Tuning: perplexity curse as a testing-effect analogue
finding: Reading documents lowers perplexity almost to 1 yet QA stays low (restudy-like), while question-formatted exposure raises QA (test-like). Machine echo of 'restudy feels fluent, retrieval works'.
numbers: PIT paper: QA 30.3 EM (7B) after standard tuning vs 48.1 with PIT++. Self-Tuning: perplexity 1.11, EM 31.52 on Wiki-Bio extraction.
limits: Analogy only, not a demonstrated mechanism. The authors do not claim it.
agent_relevance: Fluency of re-reading a context is a poor sign of usable knowledge. A scaffold should test use, not re-read.
